units.title: Unit 55 — Comparing and contrasting
learningObjectives: Express degrees of similarity and difference through precise, idiomatic collocations.
Compare benefits, risks and competing perspectives without confusing intensity and direction.
Select natural contrasts for formal analysis and everyday discussion.

items.example: The two proposals are fundamentally similar despite their different presentation styles.
items.note: Fundamentally indicates similarity in essential characteristics rather than surface details.

items.example: The finished building bears little resemblance to the original sketch.
items.note: Bear resemblance to is the conventional rather formal pairing; little emphasises dissimilarity.

items.example: The second candidate suggested an entirely different approach to the problem.
items.note: Entirely strengthens different and rules out substantial similarity.

items.example: In marked contrast to the previous quarter, sales rose in every region.
items.note: Marked contrast highlights a conspicuous difference, often in formal comparison.

items.example: The survey revealed wide variation in how families organise their working week.
items.note: Wide variation indicates substantial differences across a range of cases.

items.example: An experienced mentor can make a world of difference to a new employee.
items.note: A world of difference is emphatic and often used with make or there is.

items.example: The policy draws a clear distinction between personal and commercial use.
items.note: Clear distinction identifies a difference that is easy to recognise or define.

items.example: A yawning gap remains between the resources available to the two schools.
items.note: Yawning intensifies gap, especially for large social or economic inequalities.

items.example: The estimates differ widely depending on the assumptions used.
items.note: Widely modifies differ to indicate a considerable degree of variation.

items.example: The manager expected resistance, but the response was the exact opposite.
items.note: Exact opposite asserts a direct reversal, not a small difference.

items.example: Their approaches to leadership are polar opposites in almost every respect.
items.note: Polar opposites refers to two positions or things at opposite extremes.

items.example: For this project, the long-term benefits outweigh the disadvantages.
items.note: Outweigh expresses a judgement that one set of factors carries greater importance.

items.word: the other side of the argument
items.example: Before we vote, I would like to hear the other side of the argument.
items.note: Use this expression to invite an alternative perspective in a discussion.

items.example: The updated interface is strikingly different from the earlier design.
items.note: Strikingly conveys an immediately noticeable difference.

items.example: The smaller museum can certainly bear comparison with the city gallery.
items.note: Usually in positive or negative statements about whether two things are comparable in quality.

items.example: The new battery compares favourably with more expensive alternatives.
items.note: Compare favourably with indicates that something performs well in a comparison.

items.example: A minor scheduling delay pales in comparison with the disruption caused by a power failure.
items.note: Pale in comparison means seem much less important or impressive than something else.

items.example: The lecturer drew a comparison between learning a language and training for a race.
items.note: Draw a comparison introduces an explicit parallel between two subjects.

items.example: The team needs to strike the right balance between speed and accuracy.
items.note: Strike a balance means achieve an appropriate compromise between competing demands.

items.pt: reduzir a distância entre dois grupos ou situações
items.example: The scholarship scheme aims to bridge the gap between talent and opportunity.
items.note: Bridge the gap suggests reducing or overcoming an existing separation.

items.example: There is a subtle distinction between being confident and sounding arrogant.
items.note: Subtle distinction highlights a difference that may be hard to notice.

items.example: Economists warned about the growing disparity between regional incomes.
items.note: Disparity describes inequality; growing signals that the inequality is increasing.

items.example: The new method is fundamentally different from the one it replaced.
items.note: Fundamentally different concerns an essential difference, not merely a visible one.

items.example: There is a subtle difference between asking for guidance and avoiding responsibility.
items.note: Subtle indicates a difference that is real but not immediately obvious.

items.example: The panel listened carefully to both sides of the argument before deciding.
items.note: Both sides refers to opposing positions and supports a balanced discussion.

items.example: The quiet morning stood in stark contrast to the noisy evening.
items.note: Stark contrast emphasises a sharp, unmistakable opposition.

items.example: The first estimate was optimistic; the revised forecast was in sharp contrast.
items.note: Sharp contrast is a strong alternative to marked or stark contrast.

items.example: The two neighbourhoods contrast dramatically in the amount of green space available.
items.note: Dramatically increases the perceived scale of a contrast.

items.example: The maintenance costs may outweigh the benefits of keeping the old system.
items.note: Outweigh the benefits describes costs or risks judged greater than advantages.

items.example: The expected gains might outweigh the risks of expanding overseas.
items.note: The benefits or gains can outweigh the risks when they are judged more valuable.

items.example: A discussion about online privacy revealed a generation gap within the family.
items.note: Generation gap refers to differences in attitudes between age groups.

items.example: The entrepreneur spotted a gap in the market for affordable repair services.
items.note: This commercial expression describes a demand that existing suppliers have not met.

items.example: The two independent reports reached strikingly similar conclusions.
items.note: Strikingly can modify similar as well as different to mark an unexpected resemblance.

items.example: There is still a wide gap between the promised reforms and the actual results.
items.note: Wide describes the size of a gap, whereas bridge the gap describes an attempt to reduce it.

units.title: Unit 56 — Making an effort
learningObjectives: Distinguish individual, collective, brave and unsuccessful attempts using appropriate collocations.
Use conventional verb–noun patterns for giving advice, persevering and achieving results.
Choose accurate idioms for the difficulty, outcome and value of sustained effort.

items.example: The researchers made a determined effort to replicate the unexpected result.
items.note: Make an effort is the natural verb–noun partnership, not do an effort.

items.example: Several departments made a concerted effort to reduce unnecessary delays.
items.note: Concerted often implies coordinated, purposeful action by several people.

items.example: The successful exhibition was a joint effort by the artists and the local library.
items.note: Joint emphasises responsibility shared by two or more parties.

items.example: Finishing the installation ahead of schedule was a genuine team effort.
items.note: Team effort stresses cooperation within a group rather than individual achievement.

items.example: Despite the injury, the runner made a valiant effort to complete the course.
items.note: Valiant recognises courage or determination despite difficult conditions or failure.

items.example: The rescue crews made strenuous efforts to reach the isolated village.
items.note: Strenuous emphasises the energy or intensity required by sustained attempts.

items.example: You may not win the competition, but you should give it your best shot.
items.note: An informal encouragement to make the strongest attempt you can.

items.example: The explorers abandoned their abortive attempt to cross the glacier.
items.note: Abortive is a formal adjective describing an attempt that fails to achieve its aim.

items.example: The doctor advised avoiding intense physical exertion for a few days.
items.note: Physical exertion refers to energetic bodily activity rather than mental concentration.

items.example: Completing the final chapters was a hard slog, but the book was worth finishing.
items.note: Informal expression for long, difficult, tiring work.

items.example: Convincing investors without a working prototype will be an uphill struggle.
items.note: Suggests difficult progress against resistance with no guaranteed success.

items.example: The updated software should provide a solution to the recurring connection problem.
items.note: Provide a solution is commonly followed by to when specifying a problem.

items.example: Restoring the historic building will require considerable effort.
items.note: Require effort focuses on the work demanded by a task, not on the attempt itself.

items.example: She decided to devote more energy to improving her communication skills.
items.note: Devote energy to takes a noun or an -ing form after the preposition to.

items.example: You should follow professional advice before changing your medication.
items.note: Follow advice means act according to a recommendation; advice is uncountable.

items.example: The sailors heeded the warning and returned to the harbour.
items.note: Heed is more formal than listen to and means take a warning seriously.

items.example: After years of practice, she finally began to reap the rewards of her dedication.
items.note: Reap the rewards metaphorically means receive the benefits of previous effort.

items.example: He ignored the advice of the safety officer and entered the restricted area.
items.note: Ignore advice means choose not to act on guidance; it contrasts with heed or follow.

items.example: Without reliable funding, the expansion plan appeared doomed to failure.
items.note: Doomed to failure describes an outcome viewed as almost certain to fail.

items.pt: um desejo desesperado de ter sucesso
items.example: Her desperate desire to succeed sometimes made it hard for her to rest.
items.note: Desperate intensifies desire; the infinitive identifies the desired achievement.

items.example: Do not pin your hopes on a single interview; keep applying for other positions.
items.note: Pin your hopes on indicates relying strongly on a particular future possibility.

items.example: The simple design has stood the test of time for more than fifty years.
items.note: This fixed expression means remain effective or respected over a long period.

items.example: The repair might not work, but it is certainly worth a try.
items.note: Worth a try suggests that an attempt is reasonable despite uncertain success.

items.example: I signed up for a workshop on giving constructive feedback.
items.note: Sign up for means register to take part in a course, workshop or event.

items.example: After opening her own studio, she never looked back.
items.note: An idiom meaning achieve continued success after an important change.

items.example: If everyone makes an effort, we can finish the move before sunset.
items.note: The correct collocation is make an effort rather than do an effort.

items.example: Local volunteers made strenuous efforts to preserve the endangered woodland.
items.note: Make combines naturally with strenuous efforts; plural efforts highlights repeated action.

items.example: Learning the new programming language was demanding but worth the effort.
items.note: Worth the effort judges the result valuable enough to justify the work invested.

items.example: The underdogs made a valiant effort to stay in the tournament.
items.note: A valiant effort praises determination even if the overall goal is missed.

items.example: The career adviser offered advice on preparing a portfolio.
items.note: Offer advice is idiomatic; the noun advice does not normally take a plural -s.

items.example: A long walk by the coast always works up an appetite.
items.note: Work up an appetite means become hungry through activity.

items.example: Teams that invest in training often reap the benefits over time.
items.note: Reap the benefits is a close productive pairing to reap the rewards.
